idiom_name: raise with a dedicated exception class (no assert in core)
implementation_notes: Ruby core has no assertion facility; the idiom is an always-on guard that raises - raise ArgumentError or a small custom exception (class InvariantError < StandardError) at the top of a method for preconditions and after each mutation for object state. The runtime is never compiled away, so these checks always run; the tradeoff is that ordinary exceptions are catchable, and Minitest's or RSpec's assertion methods (assert_equal, expect(...).to eq) belong to the test suite, not production objects. A private check_invariant predicate plus candidate-state validation keeps the classic structure readable.
code_sketch:
class Account
  class InvariantError < StandardError; end

  def initialize(floor, balance = 0)
    @floor, @balance = floor, balance
    check_invariant
  end

  def withdraw(amount)
    raise ArgumentError, "amount must be positive: #{amount}" unless amount.positive?
    new_balance = @balance - amount
    raise InvariantError, "balance #{new_balance} < floor #{@floor}" if new_balance < @floor
    @balance = new_balance
    check_invariant
  end

  private

  def check_invariant
    raise InvariantError, "balance #{@balance} < floor #{@floor}" if @balance < @floor
  end
end
pitfalls: rescue StandardError around a broad block silently swallows invariant violations unless the failure class hierarchy distinguishes them from ordinary errors.
There is no debug/release switch, so heavy invariants are paid for on every call; move expensive checks into tests or a consistency job.
A bare raise "message" produces RuntimeError, which is impossible to distinguish from a genuine bug; always name the failure with a dedicated exception class.
